planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate considerably more sun than bigleaf types.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate far more direct sun than bigleaf types and are not affected by soil pH the way blue-and-pink mophead hydrangeas are. Phantom produces some of the largest flower panicles of any hydrangea cultivar, often 12–15 inches long, opening creamy white and aging to a soft pinkish blush, on a large, sturdy shrub whose thick stems hold the huge flower heads upright without flopping even after rain. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's flowers, making size management straightforward for such a large-flowered cultivar. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their full mature width to develop. Moonrock is a compact panicle hydrangea bred for exceptionally sturdy, thick stems that hold its dense, rounded flower panicles fully upright without staking, even after heavy rain — a common problem with older, larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Flowers open creamy white in mid to late summer and age to a soft green before finishing pink-blushed in fall, giving a long season of changing color on a plant sized for smaller foundation plantings and mixed borders. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Zinfin Doll Hydrangea (Deep Pink-Red Aging Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to reach its full 5–7 foot mature size. Zinfin Doll produces large, dense flower panicles that open white and quickly begin blushing pink, deepening over the following weeks to a rich wine-red by late summer and fall — a faster and more intense color transition than many other panicle hydrangea cultivars — on strong stems that hold the heavy flower heads upright. Its long season of shifting color, from white through pink to deep red, gives it multiple distinct looks across a single growing season on one plant. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Strawberry Sundae Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Red Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their mature width to fill in. Strawberry Sundae produces conical flower panicles that open creamy white and quickly flush strawberry-pink from the base upward, creating a two-toned, sundae-like effect as the color moves up each flower cluster through summer, eventually deepening to a richer rose-red in fall. Its mid-size, well-branched habit fits mixed borders and foundation plantings without the bulk of larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's flowers; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: White Diamonds Hydrangea (Sturdy Upright White Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to reach its full mature size as a large specimen shrub or small tree form. White Diamonds bears large, conical, pure white flower panicles on strong, rigid stems that stay upright through summer storms without staking, aging to a soft pink blush by fall. Its vigorous, well-branched, tree-like habit can be trained as a small single- or multi-stem specimen tree as well as grown as a large shrub, giving it more design flexibility than more compact panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun; native to Gulf South woodlands and resents heavy, poorly drained clay.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Varnadoe is a selected form of Piedmont azalea (Rhododendron canescens), a widespread Gulf South and Southeastern native, chosen for an especially heavy flush of fragrant, pale pink flowers with prominent, showy stamens on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub in early spring before the leaves fully emerge. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it is far better adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Deep South gardens than most Asian evergreen azalea hybrids, and its intense honeysuckle-like fragrance carries well beyond the plant itself. Site it at a woodland edge or under high pine or hardwood canopy, similar to the conditions where it grows wild along stream banks and bluffs.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Mount Cuba Center — Native Azalea Research

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to morning sun.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun, mulching well to keep roots cool. One of the most celebrated Exbury hybrid deciduous azaleas, Gibraltar bears large, ruffled, brilliant orange flowers with a bold yellow-orange flare and a light fragrance, opening in vivid trusses that cover the shrub in mid to late spring and rank among the most eye-catching colors in the deciduous azalea group. Fall color adds a second season of interest, with the foliage turning shades of orange, red, and purple before dropping. Site it where the intense flower color has room to make a statement — as a woodland-edge specimen or backdrop to a shade border — and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: My Mary Azalea (Golden-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. My Mary is a Southern-bred native azalea hybrid prized for its clear golden-yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance, opening in a dense spring flush on a rounded, well-branched shrub that stays more compact than many native deciduous azalea species. Its clean yellow color and fragrance, combined with better heat tolerance than many Asian azalea hybrids, have made it a favorite for Southern woodland gardens wanting a native-type azalea in a warm color outside the typical orange-to-red native range. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Mount Cuba Center — Native Azalea Research

common_name: Admiral Semmes Azalea (Golden-Orange Southern Heritage Native Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Admiral Semmes is a long-cultivated Southern heritage selection of native azalea grown for its fragrant, golden-orange flowers that open in a heavy spring flush on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub well adapted to Deep South heat and humidity. As with other native deciduous azaleas, its strong fragrance and heat tolerance have kept it in cultivation among Southern native-plant collectors even as flashier Asian evergreen azalea hybrids have dominated the broader nursery trade. Site it at a woodland edge or beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Little Devil Ninebark (Dwarf Dark-Purple Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in any well-drained to moist, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; the dark foliage color holds best in full sun.

directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Little Devil is a true dwarf ninebark selection, staying under 4 feet tall and wide — roughly a third the size of the straight species and more compact than even 'Diabolo' or 'Summer Wine' — while still producing the same deep purple-black foliage and clusters of small white to pale-pink spring flowers that draw native pollinators. Its small scale makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller mixed borders where full-size dark-leaf ninebark cultivars would be too large. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous.

common_name: Amber Jubilee Ninebark (Multicolor Orange-Gold-Red Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in any well-drained to moist, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; multicolor foliage effect is strongest in full sun.

directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Amber Jubilee stands apart from the many purple- and burgundy-leaved ninebark cultivars by cycling through a distinct multicolor foliage display: new growth emerges bright orange-gold, matures through yellow-green, and finishes deep burgundy-red by fall, often showing several of these colors on the same plant at once. Its vigorous, upright habit and season-long shifting color make it a strong focal point in a mixed shrub border. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous and colorful.
